description:
Box Elder (Acer negundo), photographed along Coyote Creek in San Jose, CA.  This is a actually a member of the genus Acer, which contains all of the North American maples, including the Sugar Maple and Red Maple of the East Coast.  However, unlike the maples with their palmately lobed leaves, Box Elder has these compound leaves, with three leaflets each.  All of the leaflets are toothed, with the terminal leaflet sometimes having two side lobes (as shown here in the lead shot). 

The tree itself is shown in the second shot of the set.  This tree is relatively modest in stature, with fairly smooth bark and a somewhat spreading habit.  Most of its summer leaves have actually turned varying shades of yellow and brown, but here and there, one can see a splash of green from some young leaves.  These younger leaves have emerged over the last few weeks because the weather has been unusually warm.

description:
This Box Elder roots on the property of the Macoskey center to the right of the Harmony Barn.
The Box Elder is a small to medium-sized tree with a short trunk and a rounded crown. It will stand from 30-60 feet tall with a diameter of 2 1/2 feet. The leaves are ovate or elliptical, saw-toothed, opposite and pinnately compound. This tree is in the same family as the Maple. You can tell by the "helicopter" seed pods that are also found on Maples

The white spots on the leaves show that this box elder has powdery mildew disease. This disease, if rapidly growing, will stop photosynthesis and kill the leaves. However, powdery mildew should not be present the following year.

Living underneath the Box Elder is a heafty groundhog (Marmota monax). He/she has made two large tunnels under the roots of this tree overtime. 

Surrounding the boxelder are more boxelder

The high temperature for the day was 86 degrees Fahrenheit. The low was 56 degrees Fahrenheit. It was a beautiful sunny day with winds blowing SW at 2mph.

description:
Boxelder (Acer negundo)

12 July 2020
Elm Fork Park
Ray Roberts State Park
Denton County, Texas

Two mature Boxelders that had been in place for what appears to be many decades fell into the canoe launch channel at the park and have started the process of becoming longtime resident snags. They appear to have broken at the base and were likely brought down by their own weight. Their tree trunks and roots had also been under water for an extended period of time and recently the water level dropped and as can be seen from these images the ground around them is still saturated with moisture. And their leaves are mostly still living given their green color leading us to conclude that their falling is a recent event.

description:
iNaturalist visits Allen Park - Salt Lake City’s newest public space (seven acres) which includes riparian habitat (Emigration Creek); Opened on October 4, 2020 - SLC Public Lands Division. Allen Park was originally founded in the 1930s as a bird sanctuary. Emigration Creek (which also runs through Wasatch Hollow Open Space and Nature Preserve) helps to anchor Allen Park as a riparian habitat - which is very unique and critical for plants and wildlife in an urban setting. 

I went in for a visit on October 13, 2020 and took a preliminary inventory (partial not complete) of what could be observed on an initial walk-through. My observations are summarized as follows. Observers can see Emigration Creek flowing (that is actual water flowing) in several spots along the walkway and it passes underneath the walkway and then runs westward toward the Westminster College area across 1300 East. What is interesting is that Emigration Creek (further upstream) remains “dry” east (and north) within and of Wasatch Hollow Open Space and Nature Preserve. There is a natural spring in Wasatch Hollow Open Space which serves as a water source and feeds into the creek flowing west (and south). There were many kinds of trees: Cottonwoods, Siberia Elms, Locust, Southern Catalpa, and Box Elder Maples, and few Pines and Spruces along the walkway. Many of the Cottonwoods were very large and they ran along the creekside. I could hear several Fox Squirrels and saw one in a tree, but I was not able to take an image. There were also Peafowl on the grounds. I was not able to observe any others birds except for what I am sure were a few Black-capped Chickadees (able to identify by the calls). Temperature was 75 degrees. Winds from south-southwest at 8 mph.

description:
A Boxxlder (Acer nugundo), photographed along the banks of Mayfield Slough in Palo Alto Baylands, Palo Alto, CA.   Note that there are seven photographs in the set of pictures documenting this tree:

Shot 1:  Provides a close-up of the samara (seed pods) that were maturing on the tree when I photographed it.  Each wing of each samara was on the order of ~2cm to ~3cm long.

Shot 2: Provides a view of an entire cluster of samara dangling from the branches of the Boxelder.

Shot 3:  Shows one of the tree's mature ternate leaves.  On this tree the leaflets of the mature leaves typically ran between 8cm and 10cm long, and between 3cm and 4cm wide.  

Shot 4:  Depicts some of the tree's young twigs and leaves. 

Shot 5:  Provides a view of the tree's main trunk.  Note the relatively smooth, gray bark.

Shot 6: A broad shot of the entire tree.  This is a fairly mature tree, so it is ~25 feet in height.
